questions.prompt: Which question gets the quick answer "In Bizerte."?
questions.explanation: "Where do you live?" is right: where asks about a place, and "In Bizerte." is the quick answer that gives the place alone. "When do you live?" asks about a time, "Who do you live with?" asks about a person, and "Why do you live there?" asks about a cause.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Where ___ your grandparents live? — They live in Kairouan."
questions.explanation: "do" is right: a question about an action follows the order WH-word + do/does + subject + base verb, and "your grandparents" is plural, so the helper is do. "does" belongs to he, she and it; "did" would put the question in the past although the answer is in the present; and "is" cannot help the verb live in a question.

questions.prompt: Complete: "___ time do you spend on your homework? — Two hours a day."
questions.explanation: "How much" is right: time is uncountable, so it takes how much — How much time do you spend on your homework? "How many" only counts plural nouns such as hours or lessons, "How long" asks the same thing but works on its own, without the noun time, and "What" cannot open this question at all.

questions.prompt: Complete: "What colour eyes ___ your sister got? — She's got green eyes."
questions.explanation: "has" is right: have got agrees with its subject, and "your sister" is she, so the pattern becomes has + subject + got — What colour eyes has your sister got? "have" belongs to I, you, we and they, and the helpers "does" and "did" are never used together with got in this pattern.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Why did she ___ famous? — Because she won an Olympic medal."
questions.explanation: "become" is right: after the helper did, the verb goes back to its base form — Why did she become famous? "became" is already a past form and cannot follow did, "becomes" adds the present -s, and "becoming" cannot follow did either.

questions.prompt: You are introducing your classmate Sonia to the class. Complete: "This is Sonia. ___ favourite subject is English."
questions.explanation: "Her" is right: when you report what a classmate told you, your becomes his or her — Her favourite subject is English. "Your" still speaks to Sonia instead of speaking about her, "She" is a subject pronoun and cannot come before a noun, and "Hers" replaces a whole noun phrase, as in This dictionary is hers.
